title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #222: Gaps Between Sums of Two Squares**

Let n₁ < n₂ < ⋯ be the sequence of integers that are sums of two squares. The problem asks for bounds on the consecutive gaps n_{k+1} - n_k.

**Key Results:**
- Upper: gap ≪ n^(1/4) (Bambah-Chowla 1947)
- Lower: limsup(gap/log n) ≥ 0.868 (DEKKM 2022)
mathContext: Classical number theory: Fermat's two-square theorem, Landau's density theorem, and analytic methods for gap estimates.

title: Sum of Two Squares
content:
**IsSumTwoSquares n:** n = a² + b² for some integers a, b.

The sequence begins: 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 25, ...

Notably, 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 19, 21-24 are NOT sums of two squares.

title: Small Examples
content:
**Small sums of two squares:**
- 0 = 0² + 0²
- 1 = 1² + 0²
- 2 = 1² + 1²
- 5 = 2² + 1²
- 13 = 3² + 2²

Note: Some numbers have multiple representations (e.g., 50 = 7² + 1² = 5² + 5²).

title: Fermat's Criterion
content:
**fermat_sum_two_squares_criterion:**

For n > 0: n is a sum of two squares ⟺ every prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) divides n to an EVEN power.

**Examples:**
- 45 = 3² · 5: YES (3 appears to power 2, even)
- 21 = 3 · 7: NO (3 and 7 both appear to odd powers)
- 63 = 3² · 7: NO (7 appears to power 1, odd)

Also: primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) are always sums of two squares.

title: The Gap Function
content:
**nthSumTwoSquares k:** The k-th element (0-indexed) of the sum-of-two-squares sequence.

**gap k:** nthSumTwoSquares(k+1) - nthSumTwoSquares(k)

The consecutive difference between successive sums of two squares.

First few gaps: 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 1, 3, 3, 1, 1, 2, 5, 1, ...

The sequence is axiomatized as strictly increasing with every element being a sum of two squares.

title: Landau's Density Theorem (1908)
content:
**landau_density_theorem:**

The number of sums of two squares up to x is:
count(x) ~ cx/√(log x)

for some constant c > 0 (the Landau-Ramanujan constant ≈ 0.7642).

This means sums of two squares are sparser than primes (density 1/log x) but denser than perfect squares (density 1/√x).

title: Erdős's Lower Bound (1951)
content:
**erdos_1951_lower_bound:**

For infinitely many k:
gap_k ≫ log(n_k) / √(log log n_k)

This was the first result showing that gaps can be significantly larger than the average gap √(log n). Erdős used sieve methods to construct intervals avoiding sums of two squares.

title: Richards's Improvement (1982)
content:
**richards_1982_lower_bound:**

limsup_{k→∞} gap_k / log(n_k) ≥ 1/4

This improved Erdős's bound by showing that gaps can be as large as (1/4) log n infinitely often. The constant 1/4 was later improved to ≈ 0.868.

title: DEKKM Improvement (2022)
content:
**dekkm_2022_lower_bound:**

limsup_{k→∞} gap_k / log(n_k) ≥ 0.868

Dietmann, Elsholtz, Kalmynin, Konyagin, and Maynard used modern sieve methods and Maynard's breakthrough techniques to achieve this constant.

title: Bambah-Chowla Upper Bound (1947)
content:
**bambah_chowla_upper_bound:**

gap_k ≪ n_k^(1/4)

Between n and n + O(n^(1/4)), there is always a sum of two squares. This uses the geometric fact that lattice points (a,b) with a² + b² ≤ n are well-distributed.

The exponent 1/4 reflects the 2-dimensional nature of the problem.

title: Summary Theorem
content:
**erdos_222_summary:**

**Lower Bounds (infinitely many large gaps):**
- Erdős (1951): gap ≫ log n / √(log log n)
- Richards (1982): limsup ≥ 1/4
- DEKKM (2022): limsup ≥ 0.868

**Upper Bound (all gaps bounded):**
- Bambah-Chowla (1947): gap ≪ n^(1/4)

The summary theorem proves the conjunction of lower and upper bounds directly from the axiomatized results.
